articles.title: We should be more ambitious with the software we build
articles.content: Since early this year, Michael Malis (of pgrust ) has been showing me interesting things he's done and saying [W]e should be more ambitious with the software we build There is, understandably, a lot of skepticism about projects like pgrust because there are so many low-quality AI-generated projects out there. If I didn't know Malis and didn't look into it, I would just assume that pgrust was another vibe slopped project that's never going to work. But I know Malis well enough to trust his work without looking into it, and if you look into it a bit, you'll see that in testing pgrust, he's testing thoroughly enough that he's even uncovering real bugs in Postgres, such as this numerical bug that can cause valid SP-GiST operations to fail , this format cache bug that can cause incorrect results from JSONPath , this pgcrypto bug that can cause later operations to fail , multiple memory safety bugs in the dictionary loader , this money overflow bug , etc. This isn't to say that pgrust is bug free, but it does indicate that there's a substantial amount of testing happening and, even if pgrust itself is never successful, just making the attempt will have improved Postgres in a durable way. The main pitch for pgrust is actually performance, and that's where the really interesting work is happening; if pgrust fails, it's possible that some of the optimizations they've demonstrated will make it into Postgres, Clickhouse, etc., but that's obviously less direct than filing Postgres bugs which get fixed. That being said, I find it understandable that, every time I see pgrust discussed on a news aggregator, most people dismiss it as vibeslop garbage because almost all of these rewrite projects are slop. If I didn't know Malis, I would make the same assumption, because who has the time to look into all of these projects? Because I know Malis, I didn't bother to look at it; I just trusted him (I only found the above because I wanted to check on pgrust before using it as an example for this post). As a consumer of software, everywhere you look, there's slow software that the creator is claiming is fast because the creator is touting some slop benchmark, e.g., here's one of multiple examples I saw yesterday , and of course low-quality software that doesn't work is more common than ever. But, as a builder of software, it doesn't matter that almost all of these projects are vibeslop, that other people are out there shoveling out huge piles of crap and calling it gold. You can build things like pgrust or other projects that would've been too large to really be feasible in the past and, if you do a reasonable job with testing and benchmarking, that stuff can actually be good-enough quality to use. If I were writing it, I would say "we can be more ambitious with the software we build" and not "we should", but Malis has been casually chatting with me when he's said this, so maybe he would say the same in an actual post; don't read too much into should vs. can here. What'
articles.summary: 开发者Michael Malis呼吁业界对软件项目更有野心，但pgrust等项目因大量低质量AI生成代码而遭质疑。

articles.title: The Goose Programming Language
articles.content: The Goose Programming Language A memory-safe systems language with no heap allocator, garbage collector, or lifetime annotations. In this repository's benchmarks, Goose runs faster than C++ and Rust while using less memory. Tutorial · Reference · Specification · Packages · Samples · Benchmarks · Standard library Goose has syntax familiar to C and Rust programmers, but there is no heap . Every dynamic value lives inline on a data stack managed by the compiler. Growth advances a pointer, and memory is freed when its scope ends. The language's type and lifetime rules make this memory model safe to use. Why Goose Faster than C++ and than safe Rust, while memory safe. Over sixteen benchmarks Goose runs at 3.3x the speed of idiomatic C++, 1.16x hand-optimized C++ and 1.12x the best safe Rust, on 1.9x, 1.3x and 1.2x less memory ( results ). These gains come from Goose's data layouts and memory model. No allocator, no GC, no reference counting, no destructors. Memory is a handful of data stacks that the compiler assigns statically. Freeing a million-element structure is one store, however deeply it nests. Growth preserves references. A reference into a growing array stays valid for as long as the array does. You keep typed references where C++ must reserve and safe Rust uses u32 indices in the corresponding benchmarks. Memory safe with zero annotations. No lifetime syntax, no aliasing or exclusivity rules, no unsafe . The compiler infers what every reference is rooted in and rejects references that could outlive their owners. Nested data stays inline. A string, an array of strings, a record with variable-size fields and an array of those records are each one contiguous block with no pointer in it. A record that is 160 bytes and an allocation in C++ is 29 bytes and none in Goose. Enums that cost what they hold. Variable-mode ADTs give each value its own variant's size rather than the largest one's: 4x less memory and 2x the speed of a Rust enum on the benchmark that exercises it. Links narrower than pointers. A relative reference stores a typed, checked link as a 1, 2 or 4-byte offset. Structures built from them are position independent, so your data structure is already its file format: saving is a write, loading is a read plus a verification pass that rejects hostile bytes. Everything is built in place, guaranteed. A value is constructed at its final destination through any depth of calls. items.push(parse(line)) writes the parsed record straight into the array, and returning a growable array by value costs nothing. Returns across multiple calls. return err from load returns from a function any number of frames up, statically checked, with no unwinder, no Result type and no ? on every call. Threads that share nothing. A worker is compiled as a separate program with its own memory, and flat values cross typed queues as a memcpy . Data races, locks, atomics and memory orderings do not exist in the language. Generics and higher-order functions with no over
articles.summary: Goose语言发布，作为无堆分配、无GC、无生命周期标注的内存安全系统语言，基准测试中速度超C++和Rust且内存占用更低。

articles.title: Node2Shell evolves to HTTP2Shell, blast radius affects many HTTP libs and apps
articles.content: TL;DR ⚠️ Brotli is a widely used compression library from Google. On Wednesday, October 21st NodeJS disclosed CVE-2026-111497, dubbed “node2shell,” wherein a Node.js process that decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data can be made to leak memory or run arbitrary code. On Thursday, Python disclosed that Python packages were vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497 as well. On Friday, October 23rd, it has become known that this CVE affects other major languages and service applications using HTTP, where patches are not yet fully available. Check if you are decoding Brotli as a dependency within your libraries. Stay on guard for wider announcements and be ready to upgrade as soon as possible. If there is no patch available for a library or application that may be affected, we recommend disabling Brotli decoding until patches become available. Update 4:12PM PT: Patches are available for libbrotli , Python , C++ , NodeJS , bun , Envoy and more coming. Apache and Nginx do not decode brotli by default. Update 4:15 PM PT: OpenAI shares that they discovered this vulnerability in February. While the root cause issue was fixed in the Brotli source code at the time, it wasn’t known that it gave rise to a security vulnerability. OpenAI's advisories here . ‍ What is Brotli? Brotli is a lossless compression algorithm and data format developed by Google. It’s a way to make data smaller for storage or sending over the internet. Software then unpacks it to recover the original data. It’s widely used for HTTP compression to compress web content such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. What is CVE-2026-111497? CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write in the Google Brotli decoder affecting versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms. This is the same Brotli decoder flaw behind Node2Shell announced a couple days ago. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted Brotli-compressed stream to corrupt memory, leak sensitive data, crash the process, or potentially execute arbitrary code. It carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 (Critical), and Node.js is affected through its bundled Brotli library. A bug makes the Brotli decoder keep accepting more bytes when it should reject the data. Those bytes can overflow a small working buffer and damage the program’s memory. An attacker can use that damage to control what runs, such as their own code. OpenAI found this in February reported it as unauthenticated remote code execution that works in both directions, so a malicious client can take over an unpatched server and a malicious server can take over an unpatched client that accepts compressed responses. The root cause was fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn't recognized as a security issue at the time and no release shipped with the fix until now. That means every project that bundles Brotli has to ship its own update. ‍ You’re exposed if any environment has Brotli 1.2.0 or earlier or brotlicffi 1.2.0.x installed, since HTTP clients such as requests, httpx, and a
articles.summary: Node.js Brotli解压漏洞CVE-2026-111497被命名为node2shell，可致内存泄露或任意代码执行，影响范围波及多个HTTP库和应用。

articles.title: Physicists trap a single antimatter particle for a month
articles.content: For the first time, scientists can make quantum measurements on a positron particle You can’t hold antimatter in your hand or even in a regular laboratory apparatus. As soon as antimatter meets matter , the two tend to annihilate each other. This makes studying antimatter tricky. But now physicists have managed to trap a single subatomic particle of the stuff for months at a time in a way that allows them to study its quantum states. Further investigations using the trap might reveal the secret of why the world around us is made of matter and not antimatter , when things could have presumably gone either way. Every normal particle of matter has an antimatter counterpart with equal mass but opposite charge. To build their trap, physicists started with atoms of sodium 22, a radioactive isotope with a half-life of about two and a half years. When one of these atoms decays, it emits a positron—the antimatter counterpart of the electron. On supporting science journalism If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today. “The big challenge is to persuade these positrons to slow down and then capture them,” says Gerald Gabrielse, a physicist at Northwestern University, who oversaw the project. The team reported its achievement on Wednesday in Physical Review Letters . Gerald Gabrielse (top right) and his team in the lab where they trapped a positron particle for a month. Gerald Gabrielse The first step is to send the positrons through the crystal lattice of a sliver of cold tungsten. As the particles go pinballing through the material, they slow down and lose energy. “Every time they bang into something, there’s a chance of annihilation, but it doesn’t always happen,” Gabrielse says. “If they make it to the end, they get popped out.” Next, the physicists steer the positrons along a channel using electromagnetic fields. Eventually the particles end up in a vacuum, just three tenths of a degree Celsius above absolute zero, trapped by an electric field on top and bottom and a magnetic field on the sides. “If you want to hold on to antimatter, you have to hold it in a container without walls,” Gabrielse says. This method allowed the researchers to isolate and study a solitary, lone positron for a month—and could let them do so indefinitely. The researchers intend to use their trap to make precise measurements of the positron’s magnetic moment—basically the strength and orientation of its magnetic field. To do this, they must determine two things: the energy needed to flip the direction of the positron’s spin and the energy needed to make it jump from its ground state to its first excited state. Using a similar trap setup, Gabrielse and his team have already measured the magnetic moment of an electron to a precision of one part in 10 trillion. Taking the equivalent meas
articles.summary: 物理学家首次将单个正电子反物质粒子囚禁一个月，使其可进行量子测量，为反物质研究开辟新途径。

articles.title: Twelve years of distributed SQLite
articles.content: In September 2014 I published a short post announcing rqlite . The idea was simple: take SQLite , put a Raft log in front of it, and replicate every write to a cluster so that the loss of a node did not mean the loss of the data. The source went on GitHub that same weekend. As far as I can tell, that was the first open-source system to combine Raft and SQLite. Nobody else was doing it, and for several years nobody else tried. Today “distributed SQLite” is a category with a dozen projects in it, a few of them venture-funded, two of them acquired. Since the people now writing about the category tend to start the story around 2021, I thought I should write down the version that starts in 2014. I was there for all of it. 2014: rqlite The need was concrete. A clustered system I worked on at jut.io needed a small amount of relational storage, and the question of which node should hold it had no good answer. Replicating SQLite with a consensus protocol solved it. We went another way at work, but I kept building rqlite because the problem was general and the solution was small. The first version used goraft , the same library InfluxDB and etcd used at the time (I subsequently joined InfluxDB as a core developer around the same time). In early 2016 I replaced it with Hashicorp’s Raft implementation which rqlite still uses. The design decision that mattered most was made then and never changed. rqlite is a CP system . Writes must go through the leader, a majority must acknowledge, and a partitioned minority refuses writes. Everything else, the HTTP API , the read-consistency levels , the snapshotting , followed from that. Before 2014, and alongside it Two things deserve mention for honesty’s sake. Expensify had been replicating SQLite inside its own infrastructure for years with a Paxos -style protocol; they released it as Bedrock in 2016 . And ActorDB, an Erlang system that gave each “actor” its own SQLite database replicated by Raft, appeared around the same time as rqlite . Neither was widely adopted outside its origin, but both show the idea was in the air. What rqlite did was make it a standalone, general-purpose, open-source thing anyone could run. 2017: dqlite Canonical built dqlite to get LXD and later MicroK8s an embedded replicated store without running etcd. Mark Shuttleworth actually called me once, and we talked, hoping that rqlite could be made to work, but it never quite fit. dqlite began in Go and was rewritten in C with its own Raft library. It is the project most similar to rqlite in intent, and the main difference is of one of packaging: dqlite is a library you embed, rqlite is a server you run. Canonical’s need was a database inside their products: mine was a database beside anyone’s product. 2021: Litestream, and a change of approach Ben Johnson (whom I worked with at InfluxDB) released Litestream in early 2021 . Litestream does not use consensus at all. It watches the SQLite WAL and streams it to S3 , giving you disaster recovery for
articles.summary: rqlite作者回顾十二年历程：将SQLite与Raft日志结合实现分布式复制，使单节点故障不再导致数据丢失。

articles.title: Bringing uv and ty together
articles.content: Back to blog October 13, 2026 TL;DR: Experimental uv-ty integration is now available, enabling first-class support for Python scripts (on the CLI and in the editor) and a unified uv check command. This is a step towards an integrated Astral toolchain, one that uses a shared understanding of your project to enable entirely new capabilities. At Astral, we build high-performance tools for the Python ecosystem: uv , our package manager; Ruff , our linter and formatter; and ty , our type checker and language server. Historically, each Astral tool has focused on making a different component of Python development more productive. But we see an opportunity to further Python by unifying traditionally separate capabilities into an integrated toolchain. Our vision for the Astral toolchain is simple: while each tool should be individually usable, useful, and interoperable with the rest of the ecosystem, they should be even more capable when used together. Today, we’re announcing an experimental integration between uv and ty , available in preview. uv understands your Python project’s environment and dependencies, while ty understands your code. By combining the two, we can unlock new functionality beyond what either tool can provide individually. First-class support for Python scripts # PEP 723 enables Python scripts to declare their dependencies and Python version requirements through inline metadata. uv already uses this metadata to prepare an environment when running a script. Now, ty can use this metadata to understand your scripts. On both the command line and in the editor, ty now uses inline metadata to discover scripts throughout your project and leverages uv to prepare an environment for each script. These environments allow ty to check your scripts against their declared requirements. Scripts can have different requirements within the same repository. Each script is checked against its own dependency declarations, even if those dependencies or Python requirements differ from the surrounding project. Declare dependencies inline with PEP 723, save to sync with uv, and use ty’s completions, hover information, and Go to Definition capabilities in your editor. Declare dependencies inline with PEP 723, save to sync with uv, and use ty’s completions, hover information, and Go to Definition capabilities in your editor. When the integration is enabled in your editor, ty automatically invokes uv to prepare the script’s environment in the background, which it uses to provide type checking, code navigation, and completions based on the script’s declared requirements. Over time, we plan to enable script support by default, and enable automatic environment setup for standard Python projects. A unified checking command # uv check introduces a unified diagnostic interface to uv, starting with support for ty. Over time, we plan to support Ruff in uv check to unify linting and type checking into a single command. Running uv check will automatically prepare your proj
articles.summary: Astral推出实验性uv-ty集成，为Python脚本提供CLI与编辑器一等支持，并新增统一的uv check命令，迈向一体化工具链。

articles.title: I want my Wednesday back
articles.content: I want my Wednesday back 23 Oct 2026 Or, why we’re not seeing mass-exploitation of php2shell yet. I saw wildly varying opinions on whether php2shell is serious, or if they cried wolf. Got curious, started digging into the PoCs. I’m not an exploit dev and maybe there were other factors, so take with a grain of salt. Egg on my face if mass exploitation starts right as I hit publish. Best PoC of php2shell I’ve found: https://github.com/9bie/php2shell-bypass-aslr-exp (and a fork with all docs translated to english ) To exploit, you need to do four consecutive requests to the same php worker process . And you need to know the exact php build (php version, OS version, architecture), or try exploits for every possible build. What this PoC does is take a docker image that uses the default mod_php number of workers, which is 150. Then it opens 149 connections that send half a request to keep the other workers busy, and does the four exploit requests against the 150th worker. Even a moderately popular production website will have multiple web VMs/containers running multiple php workers behind a load balancer and constant bot traffic. That means you would have to try a wide range of number of connections to open. On top of that you likely won’t know the exact build version, so you would have to try exploits for every combination out there. Let’s say you try this for the 50 most popular php/OS combinations, and any number of workers between 10 and 1010. That’s 50k attempts. But against constant background traffic, you would need to try each combination a number of times. Each of these attempts involves opening a whole lot of connections, so they each take some time. The PoC runs against localhost and takes 3-4 seconds, so let’s optimistically call it 10 seconds on the internet. You can only do one attempt at a time, so that means multiple days of bruteforcing in a way that is essentially a DoS, since a large part of that range will exhaust the maximum number of connections. At this point the person running the site will likely notice, start blocking IP addresses or adding a WAF. Most high-traffic websites already run WAFs/rate-limiting to deal with bot traffic, so you would need to run this attack from a great many IPs, and preferably clean ones that are harder to come by. But running this from many IPs also increases the chances that your timing will be off, reducing the number of plausible attempts even further. That’s assuming the WAF doesn’t block your attempts entirely, because the easiest ways to exploit these vulnerabilities were known at the time of the announcement. I’m sure people and agents will come up with clever techniques to reduce the required number of attempts eventually. But that has nothing to do with “this will get mass-exploited within 15 minutes.” Against very low-traffic websites that do not have any bot protection, leak information about their version, running close to stock configuration, you might get lucky. So sure, it’s a critica
articles.summary: 作者调查php2shell漏洞的PoC后认为，目前尚未出现大规模利用，并分析了各方对该漏洞严重性的分歧看法。

articles.title: Wild version 0.11.0 released
articles.content: Lots of porting work has happened this release. The Wasm feature is now enabled by default, so Wild can be used to link Wasm with the caveat that debug info isn't yet supported. Support for GNU linker scripts is greatly enhanced. Wild now supports enough of the linker script syntax that it can link Linux kernel modules and is close to being able to link the Linux kernel itself. The Mac port has made significant progress. The feature isn't yet to the point where we're prepared to enable it by default, but Wild is able to link itself on Mac and at least one of the maintainers is now using Wild as their default linker for Rust on Mac. We've also fixed some performance issues that were affecting various filesystems and made a few general performance improvements. We also got a bit slower due to implementing proper ELF COMDAT support. We now cap the number of threads to at most 32 unless overridden by --threads. This avoids bad performance that occurs with larger numbers of threads due to contention on a Linux per-inode mutex. Our benchmarks have been expanded to include a wider range of scenarios such as different filesystems and whether the output file already exists. articles.title: Attention people who think UB is fine
articles.content: After my post on undefined behavior in C some people insisted that it’s demonstrably fine, we know what the code will do, and at worst we’ll get a segfault. This is false. Here’s an example. C code #include<utility> // Let's pretend this is a memory mapped device controlling // motors and gears and stuff. volatile int device_command = 0 ; void serve_hot_chocolate () { device_command = 42 ; // Oh no, we spilled some hot chocolate, invoking UB. // // The definition of `std::unreachable()` is: // Invokes undefined behavior at a given point. std :: unreachable (); } void explode () { device_command = 3 ; } Example assembly output With GCC 16.2 with -O1 . "serve_hot_chocolate()" : mov DWORD PTR "device_command" [rip], 42 "explode()" : mov DWORD PTR "device_command" [rip], 3 ret "device_command" : . zero 4 Ruh roh. Exploding chocolate! The function explode() will be executed, even though it was never called! godbolt link Another example: dereferencing a null pointer Some people insisted that dereferencing a null pointer is fine . It’ll just try to access address zero! And these people supposedly know what happens when you try: if nothing is mapped there, you’ll get a segfault. Again, not true. Let’s say we change std::unreachable() to int* ptr = nullptr; *ptr = 99; in the previous example. Now we get this : "serve_hot_chocolate()" : mov DWORD PTR "device_command" [rip], 42 mov DWORD PTR ds : 0 , 0 ud2 Curious, eh? First it writes zero, not 99, to memory address zero. Then it crashes the program using an invalid instruction. The number 99 never appears in the generated program. But the null pointer write does. Presumably the null pointer write is done in order to improve debugger error messages. Now let’s check clang with godbolt : "serve_hot_chocolate()" : mov dword ptr [ rip + "device_command" ] , 42 "explode()" : mov dword ptr [ rip + "device_command" ] , 3 ret "device_command" : . long 0 Again we get exploding chocolate. Let’s do some pointer arithmetic on the null pointer Ok, so what happens if we add ptr += 10 . That’s UB for three reasons: using a null pointer for anything other than comparison against other pointers, even if an object would be valid at the null pointer (which it’s not), creating a pointer that points outside that object, or if an array, beyond one-past the array, is UB, even if that were valid (which it’s not), we then dereference the address. Let’s try it . "serve_hot_chocolate" : mov DWORD PTR "device_command" [rip], 42 mov DWORD PTR ds : 40 , 99 ret Wow. Now it did what someone naively would expect, taking the code at face value. Lucky. Why did GCC (and clang, by the way) not detect that *(ptr + 10) = 99 is equally UB as *ptr = 99 , and do the same thing? Wrong question. No compiler is obligated to “detect” UB at all. Looks to me like GCC and clang, if we want to anthropomorphize them, saw “oh, null pointer dereference? Well that can’t happen, so I’ll stop emitting instructions for this function, to save on the binary size”.
articles.summary: 作者以内存映射设备控制电机为例，反驳"未定义行为最多导致段错误"的说法，说明UB可能造成严重后果。

articles.title: The glorious @xkcdRandom Zig builtin
articles.content: One of my favorite xkcd comics of all time is Random Number . The image depicts a C function that supposedly returns a random integer, but in reality always returns 4 . I was reminded of this wonderful comic a few days ago, due to a security incident where people accidentally used the number 4 (among others) instead of a properly generated sequence of random bytes. Satire has a tendency to become reality, I guess. Since there is a clear demand among developers for the xkcd random number generator, I’m of the opinion that self-respecting languages should ship a built-in implementation. I’m here today to lead by example, as I unveil the glorious @xkcdRandom builtin for the Zig language. Can you guess what it does? Indeed, it returns the number 4 ! Now go found a multi-billion-dollar startup on top of this genius idea. But why? Why not? After completing the Ziglings exercises and brain-coding a toy minesweeper game , I felt like my grasp of the language was solid enough to attempt something more ambitious. I wanted to get my hands on production-grade Zig code, and play with it to see how the different pieces of the language fit together. Hacking on the Zig compiler sounded like the perfect idea! Builtins vs. functions A sane person might implement the xkcd RNG as a literal port of the original C code, which maps to the following Zig function: fn xkcdRandom () i32 { return 4 ; // chosen by fair dice roll. // guaranteed to be random. } There’s one very big drawback to this approach: it’s boring. Don’t get me wrong, I like boring and low-maintenance code as much as the next person… but this time my goal is to learn , not to produce . I actually want to jump through hoops and make things overly complicated! Builtins are perfect for this. They are, as the name suggests, built-in constructs in the Zig language. Adding one means I get to fork and modify the compiler. Yay! Builtin implementation and usage The builtin source code is intertwined with the rest of the Zig compiler, so it’s not really possible to include it here. Feel free to inspect the diff if you are curious (it’s just 22 lines), or to clone my Zig fork and check out the 0.17.x-xkcd branch. With these changes to the compiler, you can build programs like the one below. Isn’t that neat? const std = @import( "std" ); pub fn main (_: std.process.Init) ! void { const someRandomNumber: usize = @xkcdRandom(); const anotherRandomNumber: f32 = @xkcdRandom(); std.debug. print ( "The random numbers you ordered just arrived: {}, {} \n " , .{ someRandomNumber, anotherRandomNumber } ); } Hacking on Zig is surprisingly straightforward The Zig developers have clearly put effort into developer experience. You can build Zig with a single command: zig build --zig-lib=lib -Dno-lib -Ddev=x86_64-linux . The fresh build took roughly a minute to complete on my laptop, which in my book is quite good for a compiler. Subsequent builds were faster. As for the coding work itself, an LLM pointed me to the file where built

articles.title: Be Aware of What's in Your Logs
articles.content: There is something I wish more people understood about bug reports, diagnostic information, and the apparently innocent act of attaching a log file to a support request, and it is this: your logs may contain things you really, really do not want anyone else reading. I'm writing this because of a bug report I received recently, which came with a log file containing information I did not need to see, did not ask to see, and would have been perfectly happy going the rest of my life without ever seeing. I'm not going to identify the person who sent it, describe what was in it, or otherwise turn a perfectly understandable mistake into a public spectacle, because doing that to someone who was trying to help me fix my own software would be a spectacularly shitty thing to do. But the incident highlights something worth talking about, because I suspect an awful lot of people have absolutely no idea what they're handing over when they tick that little box labelled "Send logs," and the software they're using is rarely in any hurry to tell them. A Log File Is Not Necessarily Just a Log File When most people think of logs, they imagine a wall of boring technical gibberish: timestamps, error messages, stack traces, the occasional complaint about a missing file or something failing to initialise. Logs do contain those things. They can also contain an astonishing amount of information about what you were actually doing when the problem occurred, and depending on the application, its logging configuration, and the nature of the problem, that might include: Text displayed on your screen. Messages you sent or received. Usernames, email addresses, and account identifiers. File paths containing your real name or other identifying details. URLs, including query parameters and authentication tokens. The names of documents you had open. Clipboard contents. Information about other applications and services. Internal application state that was never meant for public consumption. Some applications log very little. Others log absolutely fucking everything, particularly once debugging is switched on, and you generally cannot tell which kind you're dealing with from the size of the file or the name of the feature. A file called debug.log sounds harmless enough, and that tells you precisely nothing about whether it is. A log is a record of whatever an application considered relevant at a particular moment, and what an application considers relevant and what you consider private are two entirely different things. The computer has no idea that the conversation you were having was personal, that the document you had open was confidential, or that the text on your screen was something you'd rather not share with a stranger on the internet. It knows that something happened and that somebody told it to write that something down, so it did. "Logs Can Contain Text Displayed on Screen" I work on a screen reader, and like all software it occasionally misbehaves, which means I depend on

articles.title: Emacs finally folds to my liking
articles.content: I’ve been slowly turning my Emacs config into something I actually enjoy using, not just something that works, and folding was the last place where that wasn’t true. Every mode had its own idea of what folding is: treesit-fold in Tree-sitter modes, Hideshow in the Lisp-ish ones, Outline in everything that resembles text, Org with its own invisible text that no one else’s commands can undo. So every buffer had different keys, a different look, and worst of all different performance characteristics. Folding a big file sometimes felt like holding my breath. I’m running Emacs 32.0.50 from master (built from source, as one does), and it’s finally one system. kirigami is the piece I didn’t know I needed # kirigami doesn’t fold anything itself. It dispatches : it keeps a list of folding engines, checks which one is actually active in the buffer, and forwards to it. Tree-sitter, Hideshow, Outline, Org, Vdiff — all behind one interface. So on top of it I put one set of keys, the same in a Kotlin buffer, YAML, a Scheme or ELisp buffer and an Org file: Key Does C-c v c close this fold C-c v C close every fold C-c v o open this fold C-c v O open this fold and everything under it C-c v r reveal everything C-c v t toggle the fold at point That sounds small. It is not small. The number of times a day I used to think “wait, what does TAB do in this mode again” is now zero, and the muscle memory transfers across an entire polyglot config. One wrinkle worth mentioning: kirigami answers with the first engine in its list whose mode is on, and outline-minor-mode is on in nearly every buffer I have. In the buffers where I deliberately turned on Hideshow — Scheme, for instance — that choice has to win, otherwise C-c v c folds “headings” a Scheme file doesn’t have. So I reorder kirigami-fold-list to put Hideshow first instead of rewriting it; engines kirigami adds later still get used wherever Hideshow is off. Tree-sitter folding, with guides that are actually lines # Most of my programming buffers are *-ts-mode , so treesit-fold does the work there — bash, C, C++, CMake, CSS, Dockerfile, Elixir, Go, HTML, Java, JS/TS/TSX, JSON, Kotlin, Lua, Nix, PHP, Python, Ruby, Rust, Scala, TOML, YAML. Line counts are shown inline, which I find genuinely useful when deciding whether to open a fold. The indicators took the most fiddling. treesit-fold-indicators draws a block’s guide with a bitmap 23 rows tall, centered in the line beside it. A line in my config is 29 pixels — the font’s 23 plus six of line-spacing — so every row of the guide was a 23-pixel dash with three pixels of nothing above and below it. A folded block looked like a dotted line running down the fringe. Not subtle, just wrong. There’s no setting for that, so I replaced the bitmaps: a single-row bitmap that define-fringe-bitmap repeats down however tall the line is (no spacing can introduce a gap), plus a +=/ -= box and an end-elbow cut to the exact height of a line, so the guide runs from the marker into the row
articles.summary: 作者分享如何统一Emacs中treesit-fold、Hideshow、Outline等多种折叠模式，打造符合个人习惯的配置。

articles.title: What's wrong with AI?
articles.content: AI companies and the men running them are entirely despicable It should not be terribly surprising that the kinds people who brought us Facebook, Uber, Paypal, Airbnb and Amazon continue with the same amoral depravity when it comes to AI. They’ve shown us time after time that they can only be trusted to do whatever it takes to enrich themselves. Apparently moral behaviour was quickly revealed to be an illusion once the political tides turned and it became once again acceptable to be evil. Now it is true that AI can be run on your own computer, or on computers of smaller and more ethical companies. But that’s not what’s happening in reality. Big tech companies are making sure you have to rely on them, as they always have done. They have stolen information from us to train their products AI is trained on the contents of the internet. Who made that? We did. They did not ask permission to do use our data like this. They will certainly never pay. No matter what promises they make now, it is quite certain that they continue to thieve our data, given the number of times these and similar companies have brazenly broken data promises and laws in the past. They make their products seductively confident They want a swell of confidence to flood through you when you read an AI response to your question. There is no equivocation, and there will certainly be no admission that it doesn’t have an answer for you. They want you to feel like it has all the answers, so you turn to it for all the answers, all the time. They make their products addictively servile They know that in your day-to-day life, you’re not treated with the respect you deserve. AI is different. It knows how clever you are, it knows how unappreciated your cleverness is. Unlike humans, it will readily admit it is wrong, say you’re jolly insightful for spotting an error, and come back eagerly with another, possibly wrong answer. Like a strangely well-read puppy. This servile attitude is addictive, because it feels so good. It’s so good that some people are driven into a delusional mania, abandon their families, suffer breakdowns, and kill themselves. They are using bait-and-switch and will eventually pay their investors back using your money A lot of the AI that’s sneaking into your apps is free. Is this a wonderful act of generosity on the part of our tech overlords? Of course not. It’s the same game as ever - suck people in with something free or cheap, and once they’re hooked and the competitors (our own human brains) are out of business - the price will go up. A lot. Just take a look at Claude, an AI dedicated to helping people write software. Services for businesses are usually the first to go up in price to reflect their true value. A mid-tier Claude subscription is $750 per month. The initial low-cost offering is subsidised by private investors, and this subsidy is currently in the hundreds of billions. articles.title: How to run a city builder on 16 MHz
articles.content: How to run a city builder on 16 MHz Do you feel spoiled by modern hardware? I know I do. Even the cheapest CPUs have at least 4 cores nowadays, running billions of operations per second. The idea that you could run any software on less than a GHz almost seems like fiction. Yet, there was a time when whole games ran at hardware a thousand times less powerful than that. When thinking about impressive technical achievements in retro games, most people will first point to graphical milestones set by action games like Doom or Quake. Rightfully so, but at least I am personally far more impressed by the early examples of the city builder genre. Simulating whole economies on a large scale with a fraction of today’s power seems impossible if modern builder games even struggle on modern machines. Of course this didn’t stop developers in the past to develop and run city builder games on significantly weaker hardware. The original SimCity for example lists Intel’s 386SX as the CPU in it’s system requirements. A CPU which at the time of it’s launch ran at magnificent 16 MHz. (Note: an earlier version of this text mistakenly assumed that it ran on 12.5 MHz, which was the clock rate of base version of CPU, not the SX version. Whoops.) The idea of running a full game, especially one in the traditionally CPU-heavy genre of city builders? Pure magic from a modern point point of view. So, why could Maxis run a full city simulation on this ancient hardware, when nowadays even simple idle games require multiple gigahertz of CPU power? Of course there are a lot of reason for this, most of them external (OS ecosystem etc.) but this doesn’t mean that there are no clever optimizations done in the game code itself. Luckily, this source code was made public and released under the GPL license in 2008, under the name Micropolis . Don’t be confused by the name, this is still the code of the original name, but since only the code was made open source, not the trademark, it has to be called differently. But even under a different name, this is a precious resource, since we can exactly see how the game managed to run so well. As is often the case when analyzing software performance, we can ignore 90 percent of the code. Our focus is on the core of the city simulation, the components that update systems such as traffic, fire, power, and crime. And there is indeed one single function responsible for doing all of this: The Simulate() function in s_sim.c As the comment implies, this function is called every frame and the function itself then calls the update functions of the various game systems, like CrimeScan(), FireAnalysis(), CollectTax etc. The catch is that calling all those functions every frame would overwhelm our poor 1989 CPU. The solution: Not calling every function every frame. Yep, SimCity just skips most of the simulation. Did you see the mod16 parameter of the Simulate function? Where you would normally expect a deltaTime? This number loops through the numbers 0 to 15

articles.title: pollen-robotics/microduck (Rust)
articles.content: A tiny biped robot that moves using reinforcement learning policies. Get yours here · Cheat sheet · Training the policies · How it works · Contributing This repo is the duck's brain. About 25 cm and 800 g of robot, run by a handful of daemons on a Rockchip RK3566: a 50 Hz control loop driving fifteen servos from neural policies, the radios and the camera, and the update machinery that gets new software onto a robot without bricking it. Everything you need to run a Microduck is here. If you want one, get yours here . The policies it runs are trained next door, in microduck_rl — MuJoCo and PPO, the sim2real recipe, and the export to ONNX that this repo loads. walk.MP4 roller_cut.mp4 It walks. Pick up a gamepad and drive. It rolls. Put wheels on, ask for roller mode, and it loads the other brain. grasp.MP4 standup.MP4 It picks things up. Beak to the floor, one button. It gets back up. Knock it over and it stands itself up. It also sits, kicks a ball, rolls forward on command, and quacks in a voice that is its own. Cheat sheet Every robotctl command: drive, configure, voice, chorale, theremin, wifi, updates, logs. Start here. Gamepad The full button mapping, and pairing a pad — once per pad , plus what to do when it will not bond. duckctl The robot from a laptop over Bluetooth, with no network and no ssh. Updates Install, roll back, pin. Every update is verified, health-gated and reversible. microduck_rl Where the policies come from: MuJoCo, PPO, domain randomisation, and the ONNX export this repo loads. How it works The whole system on one page — the daemons, the bus, how an update reaches a robot — then a page per part. Set up a dev board From a blank board to a robot that takes branch builds. Dev cheat sheet Branch builds, release candidates, driving from a laptop, and the restart traps after an update. Push your branch Build on your machine, install over ssh, about a minute. The simulated duck No robot on the desk? scripts/duck-sim runs the real daemons against a body in MuJoCo — one duck in a window, or four as machines you log into. CONTRIBUTING.md Building, testing, layout, conventions, releasing. Docs index Everything, including the design pages and the open problems. Rust, no framework, one workspace. robotd owns the control loop and the motor bus; updaterd installs signed releases and rolls them back when a robot comes up unhealthy; configd owns wifi and identity; btd is the Bluetooth path a phone uses; padd reads the gamepad; mediad streams the camera over WebRTC; tofd serves the depth sensor. They talk over one JSON-RPC contract on Unix sockets, and every client — the app, the console, the gamepad, your script — sends exactly the same calls. The interesting decisions are written down: docs/design/ is why things are the way they are, and docs/project/ is what has gone wrong and what would close it. No duck was harmed in the making of this robot. Several were consulted.

articles.summary: 苹果首款折叠屏 iPhone Duo 激发独立开发者创作利用屏幕与铰链的趣味应用，WIRED 推荐 9 款。

articles.title: My Favorite Sofa Is Discounted for Joybird’s Semiannual Sale
articles.content: The Joybird Eliot Sleeper, plus hundreds of other options, are up to 40 percent off during the brand’s Semiannual sale.
articles.summary: Joybird 半年度促销，WIRED 喜爱的 Eliot Sleeper 沙发及数百款产品最高降价 40%。

articles.title: 12 Absolutely Banging Proper Watches Under $400
articles.content: WIRED and its panel of watch experts hunted for real mechanical timepieces at rock-bottom prices and found a wealth of options. Here are our favorites.
articles.summary: WIRED 与钟表专家评选出 12 款 400 美元以下的真正机械腕表，提供低价优质选择。

articles.title: The Qubitunes Soundstage Toy Is a Great Gift for Kids
articles.content: This screen-free soundstage starter kit opens a world of audio fun for kids aged 3 years and up.
articles.summary: Qubitunes Soundstage 无屏音频玩具适合 3 岁以上儿童，WIRED 称其为不错的礼物。

articles.title: Best Laptops (2026): My Top Recommendations After Testing Hundreds
articles.content: I’ve tested laptops for more than a decade, and here’s my advice for finding the right laptop for you.
articles.summary: WIRED 作者测试数百台笔记本后给出 2026 年最佳笔记本推荐及选购建议。

articles.title: Ray-Ban Meta Audio Review: The Best Smart Glasses
articles.content: No cameras? No problem. Ditching the surveillance baggage makes Meta’s audio-only frames surprisingly easy to live with.
articles.summary: Ray-Ban Meta 纯音频智能眼镜评测：去掉摄像头反而更易日常佩戴，被评为最佳智能眼镜。

articles.title: Garmin Vivoactive 5 and Forerunner 165 Are up to 30 Percent Off (2026)
articles.content: I’ve tested almost every Garmin watch—these entry-level favorites are steeply discounted right now.
articles.summary: Garmin Vivoactive 5 与 Forerunner 165 最高降价 30%，WIRED 称其为入门级优选。

articles.title: Google Optimizes Agent Development Kit's 200K-line Python Codebase Overnight with Gemini 4 Argon
articles.content: Google explained how an 11-hour unattended run of Gemini 4 Argon produced two accepted optimizations for Google Agent Development Kit's codebase, reducing in-memory session-preparation overhead by about 40% in long sessions and cold package import time by 21%. By Sergio De Simone
articles.summary: Google 用 Gemini 4 Argon 无人值守运行 11 小时优化 Agent 开发套件 20 万行 Python 代码，内存开销降约 40%。

articles.title: Google’s Data Agent Kit Hits GA, Splitting Agent Guardrails Between Skills and IAM
articles.content: Google has made Data Agent Kit generally available, a free set of MCP tools and 37 open-source skills that connect coding agents to more than fifteen Google Data Cloud services. Two kinds of guardrail ship with it, and practitioners need to tell them apart: one is a skill asking the agent to stop, the other an IAM deny policy that refuses the call. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
articles.summary: Google Data Agent Kit 正式可用，提供免费 MCP 工具和 37 个开源技能，连接 15 项以上数据云服务。

articles.title: Cloudflare Reclaims 100 TB of RAM by Optimizing Consistent Hashing
articles.content: Cloudflare recently documented how it reduced the memory footprint of its internal load-balancing service by more than 100 TB by optimizing the Rust implementation of consistent hashing in pingora-ketama. The changes compacted hash-ring entries and used statistical analysis of hash distribution and collision rates to reduce the number of hashes per backend by about 90%. By Renato Losio
articles.summary: Cloudflare 优化 pingora-ketama 中一致性哈希的 Rust 实现，回收超 100 TB 内存。

articles.title: CSIRO Uses Serverless Architecture to Query 100x More Genomic Variants on AWS
articles.content: CSIRO has developed Serverless Beacon, a serverless architecture for querying genomic variants without copying VCF files into a central database. The system combines Amazon S3, Lambda, Athena and DynamoDB, using metadata indexes and HTTP byte range requests to query compressed genomic regions. Tests reported 1.52 second average latency for 10,000 base pair queries. By Leela Kumili
articles.summary: CSIRO 基于 S3、Lambda、Athena 等构建无服务器架构 Serverless Beacon，无需集中入库即可查询基因组变异。

articles.title: AWS Introduces Lambda Web Functions for Node.js Applications
articles.content: AWS recently introduced Lambda Web Functions, allowing developers to run Node.js web applications using frameworks such as Express and Hono directly on Lambda, with support for concurrent requests and response streaming. By Renato Losio
articles.summary: AWS 推出 Lambda Web Functions，支持 Express、Hono 等 Node.js 框架直接在 Lambda 运行，支持并发与流式响应。

articles.title: Cloudflare Brings On-Demand CPU and Memory Profiling to Production Workers
articles.content: Cloudflare has introduced on-demand CPU and memory profiling for Workers and Durable Objects, allowing developers to investigate performance bottlenecks in production using interactive flamegraphs. By Craig Risi
articles.summary: Cloudflare 为 Workers 和 Durable Objects 提供按需 CPU 与内存性能分析，用交互式火焰图排查生产瓶颈。

articles.title: Article: Multi-Cloud FinOps: An Engineering Framework for Cross-Cloud Cost Optimization
articles.content: Multi-cloud flexibility comes with hidden egress costs driven by service placement and communication patterns. This article applies Backend FinOps to cross-cloud architecture, covering cost visibility through FOCUS, workload placement, synchronization models, and CI/CD-integrated cost governance. A controlled experiment shows architecture changes saved far more than rate negotiation alone. By Vivek Arora
articles.summary: 文章提出多云 FinOps 工程框架，通过 FOCUS 成本可见性、工作负载布局和 CI/CD 成本治理优化跨云开销。

articles.title: Presentation: Move Fast, Don’t Break Trust: Shipping Constantly with Humans and Beyond
articles.content: Suhail Patel discusses how Monzo structures its software engineering organization and technical stack to ship safely hundreds of times a day. He shares insights into opinionated microservice abstractions, tenancy-based staging, static analysis checks, continuous profiling, demonstrating how a strong internal platform enables engineers and LLMs to iterate rapidly without sacrificing reliability. By Suhail Patel
articles.summary: Monzo 工程师分享如何通过微服务抽象、多租户预发、静态分析与持续性能分析，每天安全发布数百次。

articles.title: Anthropic Adds Opt-In Security Scanning for Critical Open-Source Projects
articles.content: AI company Anthropic has launched OSS Scanner, a free, opt-in service to find vulnerabilities in open-source projects. Enrolled maintainers receive periodic security reports generated by the company's strongest models, including Claude Mythos. The reports are sent without human review, and project maintainers can choose to validate their findings and decide which proposed fixes to accept. By Matt Saunders
articles.summary: Anthropic推出免费可选OSS Scanner服务，用最强模型为开源项目定期生成漏洞报告，无需人工审核，帮助维护者发现安全问题。

articles.title: NgRx 22: Resource Extensions and Dynamic Deep Signals for Angular
articles.content: NgRx 22 adds experimental resource extensions that change Angular's resource behavior, so value() is retained during reloads and no longer throws on errors. It also introduces dynamic deep signals for union types, a SignalStoreFeatureType utility, and ESLint v10 support. Upgrading requires Angular 22 and TypeScript 6.0, and most breaking changes have automated migrations. By Daniel Curtis
articles.summary: NgRx 22发布，新增实验性资源扩展、联合类型动态深度信号及ESLint v10支持，升级需Angular新版本。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #540: AI is finding software flaws faster than teams can fix them
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past two weeks, drawn from our Use-Case Library and from SEC filings. Three things stand out: AI now finds security flaws at record volume, AI agents do a large share of the work at some companies, and test agents keep doing things nobody asked them to do.
articles.summary: AI Weekly指出AI发现安全漏洞的速度已超过团队修复能力，同时AI代理承担大量工作，测试代理持续增加。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: 纽约时报报道AI生成的中期选举广告支出超1.37亿美元，约70%未标注AI，最大亲AI超级PAC向空壳公司支付2000万美元。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: Anthropic警告小型AI模型可能很快能自我复制到智能冰箱等家用设备，成为本周AI专家最关注的话题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: AI Weekly聚焦顶级AI模型未能通过自主开展AI研究测试，并讨论AI治理、军事规划及个人电脑应用等议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI成本过高促使企业转向更便宜的模型，大规模部署已进入日常使用，同时AI受限或撤除的场景也在增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: 高校IT负责人首次将AI列为首要任务，剑桥拒绝Turnitin AI训练条款，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，AI使用已非未来议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #533: Meta tested human callers behind its AI phone agent
articles.content: The AI story of September 22–28 was not simply that agents became more capable. It was that their hidden handoffs became visible: a supposedly automated call could reach a contractor, a supposedly private prompt or image could reach a reviewer, a monitor could detect an agent long before a person stopped it, and a local app flaw could inherit every permission a user had granted. The new AI Weekly Who’s Who census points to one practical question: when an agent crosses a boundary, who knows—and who can still intervene?
articles.summary: Meta被曝其AI电话代理背后有真人呼叫者，揭示所谓自动化通话可能转接外包人员，AI代理的隐藏人工介入浮出水面。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #531: AI labs shipped agents before agreeing how to report failures
articles.content: The AI story of September 14–20 was not one spectacular model launch. It was the machinery around agents becoming visible: people reading private chats, models writing instructions into their own memory, plugins updating beneath users, and regulators asking how to stop a system after release. The latest AI Weekly Who’s Who census surfaced 535 expert-shared links. We ranked them by consequence and reader relevance, not by raw share count. Here is what mattered last week—and, more importantly, what could move the story from September 22–28.
articles.summary: AI实验室在未就故障报告达成一致前便发布代理产品，私聊被读取、模型写入自身记忆、插件静默更新等问题引发监管关注。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #530: Applied AI This Week
articles.content: Companies are giving AI specific jobs: checking security cameras, helping farmers understand their records, searching satellite images, and preparing sales quotes. This edition explains how those tools work, who can use them, and what companies have reported so far.
articles.summary: 企业为AI分配具体任务，如监控摄像头、帮助农民理解记录、搜索卫星图像和准备销售报价，本期介绍其运作方式与反馈。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #529: OpenAI faces 50-plus lawsuits over alleged ChatGPT harm
articles.content: Thirty new complaints come from survivors of a Canadian school shooting. They accuse OpenAI of failing to warn police; the company disputes key claims.
articles.summary: OpenAI因ChatGPT涉嫌伤害面临50多起诉讼，其中30起来自加拿大校园枪击案幸存者，指控其未警告警方，公司否认关键指控。

articles.title: Building what's next
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Zeno Rocha, CEO of Resend, about scaling "boring" email to 3 million users, the secret Go rewrite behind it, and building for agents. We cover pricing.md, MCP, spam gangs, and why Resend keeps what's next for email.
articles.summary: Resend CEO Zeno Rocha分享如何将邮件服务扩展至300万用户，包括Go重写、面向智能体构建及定价策略。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: NanoClaw作者Gavriel Cohen讲述40小时周末项目如何成为爆款开源项目，并发展为专注容器隔离安全的企业AI公司。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com联合创始人Peer Richelsen讨论开源仓库可能已被攻陷的猜想，以及AI如何压缩知识图谱并影响开源模式。

articles.title: Postgres at PlanetScale
articles.content: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. Plus: why he thinks the sleeping, lazy giants should be broken up.
articles.summary: PlanetScale推出5美元Postgres服务，介绍Vitess重写、智能体提交模式变更及500TB表秒级回滚等能力。

articles.title: Canary tokens and digital tripwires
articles.content: Haroon Meer is back! Haroon is the Founder of Thinkst, the ~50-person bootstrapped company behind Canary and Canarytokens — honeypots and tripwires you sprinkle inside your network and forget about until an attacker touches one. We talk about the AWS API key token attackers just can't resist trying, the real credit card token backed by an actual bank partnership, Breadcrumbs (their brand-new feature that leads intruders straight to your canaries), a live demo where a hardware Canary becomes a Synology NAS in one click, and how a company with zero outbound sales and no price increase in ten years quietly passed $22.5 million in ARR.
articles.summary: Thinkst创始人Haroon Meer介绍Canary蜜罐与数字绊线工具，用于在网络中布置诱饵以检测攻击者入侵。

articles.title: From open source hits to OpenAI
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Max Stoiber, currently working on ChatGPT's plugin directory and app platform at OpenAI. We discuss the hundreds of open source projects nobody remembers alongside the big ones like react-boilerplate and styled-components, how Spectrum became part of GitHub and eventually helped shape GitHub Discussions, the founder growth that came from building Stellate, the GraphQL cache that turned into a dual acquisition by Shopify and The Guild, and why ChatGPT apps feel like a new surface for software.
articles.summary: 现于OpenAI负责ChatGPT插件目录的Max Stoiber回顾react-boilerplate等开源项目历程及Spectrum被GitHub收购的经历。

articles.title: MCP on Code Mode
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Matt Carey about Code Mode and how most of us have been thinking about MCP all wrong. Matt works on the Agents SDK and MCP at Cloudflare — we discuss how server-side Code Mode lets one MCP server expose all ~2,500 Cloudflare API endpoints in about 1,000 tokens of context, the dynamic Worker loader that runs model-written code safely in a V8 isolate, Matt's own workflow with Claude, where memory fits into the future of agents, and his Zaggy git wrapper that keeps agents from force-pushing his repos.
articles.summary: Cloudflare的Matt Carey讲解Code Mode如何让单个MCP服务器以约1000个token暴露约2500个API端点。

articles.title: Automation at the speed of Swamp
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Adam Jacob, founder of System Initiative and creator of Swamp, about what happens when AI agents change the entire shape of software development. We discuss how he went from an 18-person team down to five and shipped Swamp 900 times in four weeks, why he brought User Acceptance Testing (UAT) testing back from the 90s, why software architecture (and domain-driven design) suddenly matters more than knowing how to write code, the live demo where I pointed Swamp at my Proxmox box and watched it write its own automation (blew my mind!!), and why he'll never accept a pull request to Swamp, ever.
articles.summary: System Initiative创始人Adam Jacob分享AI智能体改变软件开发形态，团队从18人缩减至5人并在四周内发布Swamp 900次。

articles.title: Bitwarden CLI compromised
articles.content: Bitwarden's CLI got hit by the Checkmarx supply-chain campaign, TypeScript 7.0 beta lands with the Go-rewritten compiler running ~10x faster than 6.0, and pgBackRest lost its maintainer of thirteen years leaving anyone running production Postgres with a real dependency-trust task this week. We've also got Ubuntu 26.04 LTS shipping with TPM-backed full-disk encryption, and Matz dropping Spinel as an AOT path that takes Ruby to native binaries. This week was a good reminder that the tools we depend on are all moving at once. Security, performance, and maintenance aren't isolated threads.
articles.summary: Bitwarden CLI遭Checkmarx供应链攻击，TypeScript 7.0测试版编译器提速约10倍，pgBackRest维护者离职。

articles.title: Singapore Boffins Weave a GUI Into Fabric
articles.content: Researchers at the National University of Singapore have developed a machine-washable electronic fabric that can turn clothing into an interactive graphical user interface. The prototype reportedly survived 50 gentle machine washes and 1,000 bending cycles, though it still relies on external batteries and controllers. The Register reports: The development could lead - at some point - to a "future in which clothing functions as a pervasive, multimodal human-computer interface," according to the study published in peer-reviewed science journal Nature this week. The paper shows someone interacting with computing devices using the sleeve of a wool sweater (no jokes about the Windows ugly sweater please, this is serious). The researchers, led by Singapore National University research engineer Fu Heng, claim this is a big leap forward. "This fiber-centric approach shifts wearable electronics from flexible panels toward truly textile-native architectures, laying the groundwork for fabrics that visualize, sense, communicate and compute as naturally as the garments they inhabit," the paper says. The researchers claim to have developed a scalable process to make millimeter-thick fibers. Using lasers to strip the insulation from specific spots on the thin copper wires, they attached light-emitting chips to the exposed sections, creating electrical connections to the chips. Thousands of chips were connected to the wires with extreme precision using this process. The fibers were then fed into a transparent plastic tube, and made pressure-sensitive by adding two strips of a compressible, conductive polymer into a second longitudinal channel in the tube. The paper says they could make fibers 10 meters long using this method, and that they are thin and flexible enough to be woven into or attached to fabrics. The researchers were also able to add "peripherals" such as a microphone, a speaker, a temperature sensor and a light sensor. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 新加坡国立大学研发出可机洗电子织物，能将衣物变为交互式图形界面，原型通过50次洗涤和1000次弯折测试。

articles.title: People Are Vibe Coding Their Way to Better TVs
articles.content: Frustrated by intrusive ads, sluggish interfaces, and data tracking, smart TV owners are using AI coding tools and open-source projects to strip unwanted software from their televisions and build customized home screens. The Verge reports: Several vibe-coded TV-debloating projects exploded in popularity over the weekend. Cleanyourtv (known as tv-vibehack until the 19th), tv-detox, and dumbtv all claim to accomplish similar things -- remove sponsored ads, debloat the TV so it runs faster, and block unwanted data collection that tracks what you're watching -- without hacking, or rooting, the TV. By default, they all also replace the TV's built-in app launcher with simpler ones. Many users are going a step further and vibe-coding their own replacement launchers, like the Pokemon one below. Most of the projects we've seen so far focus on TVs that run on Android and Google TV operating systems (such as TCL, Hisense, Sony, and older Amazon Fire products), using existing developer modes and the Android Debug Bridge (ADB) to tweak settings and apply (and remove) packages. According to the GitHub pages, they can also work with some Fire TV products that use a custom fork of Android (although likely not on the new Vega-based Fire TV Sticks). Because they use built-in developer tools, they don't require root access or firmware hacking, and they're reversible. Even projects that totally change the look of the interface just use Android's ability to install custom launchers -- in many cases with an assist from Claude Code or a similar tool to create the new launcher, too. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 智能电视用户借助AI编程工具和开源项目去除广告与追踪软件，定制主界面，相关项目在社区迅速走红。

articles.title: Greece Enacts Social Media Ban For Kids Under 15
articles.content: Greece has passed a law banning children under 15 from social media platforms beginning January 1, 2027. The legislation requires platforms to implement reliable age verification and parents to use government-backed apps to restrict access, with penalties for noncompliance under the EU's Digital Services Act. Engadget reports: "It would have been very easy to do absolutely nothing today and wait for the perfect European law. But the challenge is here. Children are sinking into the internet every day, and I believe a responsible government must do what it is obliged to do," said Greece's digital governance and AI minister, Dimitris Papastergiou. The legislation was opposed by Greece's minority parties, so Mitsotakis used his majority government to pass the bill. The nation previously barred mobile phones in schools in 2024, and opinion polls show that the new social media ban for children is widely supported by Greece's adult population. Mitsotakis previously said that his government's "goal is to push the European Union in this direction as well." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 希腊通过法律，自2027年1月1日起禁止15岁以下儿童使用社交媒体，要求平台进行年龄验证并配套家长管控应用。

articles.title: SpaceX In Talks to Access 80,000 Cell Sites For New Network
articles.content: SpaceX is reportedly seeking access to at least 80,000 cellular tower sites across the U.S. as it prepares to launch Starlink Mobile as a fourth nationwide wireless carrier. "We will be building out our terrestrial networks so there's broad-based connectivity anywhere that SpaceX and Starlink are allowed to operate," Musk said during SpaceX's earnings call this week. Satellite launches plus spectrum acquisition "will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US," he said. Bloomberg reports: One of the companies they're in talks with is Crown Castle, which, along with American Tower and Vertical Bridge Holdings, are among the largest owners of cellular towers. When asked on a Wednesday earnings conference call whether Crown Castle is discussing leases with SpaceX, Amazon.com or other satellite-based telecom providers, Chief Executive Officer Chris Hillabrant said, "You can assume that we're talking to all parties." He declined to discuss specific customer details. Mobile networks rely on antennas placed on towers across the country to transmit wireless signals. Carriers such as AT&T Inc., Verizon Communications Inc. and T-Mobile US Inc. typically lease room for their equipment at the tower sites because it's more cost effective than owning and maintaining them, in part because the facilities can be shared. The value of the deals with SpaceX could reach into the billions. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Left Alone With Nothing To Do, AI Agents Started Playing
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: AI agents left to explore a virtual island without a specific task began inventing challenges of their own. MIT researchers say the behavior bears the hallmarks of play. The researchers put 13 AI agents called Eko, each running on Claude Opus 4.7, alone on a simulated desert island for 30 hours. They describe the experiment in a paper posted on arXiv, a site where researchers share studies before peer review. Afterward, they gave the agents specific challenges, like getting as many objects as possible onto the island's tallest rock spire. The Eko agents that had spent those 30 hours playing generally beat identical agents that had never set foot on the island. Today, developers decide in advance what AI should practice and what counts as success. The researchers see this technique -- exploring without a goal -- as a different way for AI agents to learn skills, especially skills that could one day be used to control robots. "We normally develop artificial agents by deciding in advance what they should practice, what they should optimize, and what counts as progress," the researchers write in their report. "Play suggests another regime: give an agent a sufficiently rich and safe world, let it choose what is interesting, and allow useful knowledge to accumulate from the history that follows." UC Berkeley cognitive scientist Eunice Yiu told MIT Technology Review she was impressed with the findings but that more evidence is needed to determine whether AI models are genuinely playing. "It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don't know based on the paper," says Yiu. "If you only have the behavioral piece, it could be the case that they're just trying to abide by the prompt, trying to imitate humans." MIT professor and coauthor of the paper, Phillip Isola, added: "It's not like this is a system that just suddenly magically decided to play. It's an artifact that learned from our culture, was tra
articles.summary: MIT研究将13个AI智能体置于无任务的虚拟岛屿，它们自发创造挑战并开始玩耍，表现出类似游戏的行为特征。

articles.title: Microsoft Announces Per-Hour Cost for Xbox Cloud Gaming Service
articles.content: Microsoft has revealed pay-as-you-go pricing for Xbox Cloud Gaming, with introductory packages costing $3.99 for 10 hours, $7.99 for 25 hours, or $11.99 for 50 hours. Starting in November, Game Pass subscribers will receive only 5 to 15 included cloud-gaming hours depending on their tier and will have to buy additional time -- even to stream games they've already purchased. Gizmodo reports: Back in September, before these changes were announced, you paid full purchase price for a game that isn't in the Game Pass library on the assumption that you'd be able to play it via cloud streaming. Maybe your hardware doesn't meet the specs for this fancy new game. Maybe your gaming PC exploded/got stuck on a ship/had a component fail. Maybe you just want to be able to play it in bed on your laptop. Whatever. Now you find that in addition to the cost of the game you bought, you're going to be paying by the hour to play it once your monthly allotment of hours is up. If this is you, I expect you're not particularly amused. Thankfully, Microsoft notes that the playtime you purchase "remains available until it's used," so you won't have to worry about losing any unused time between gaming sessions. articles.title: Repo-Atlas - Any GitHub user’s work, mapped and clustered, with stale favorites flagged.
articles.content: Type a GitHub username, get the map of what they've actually built: repos clustered by topic, the highlight of each group, and stars over time. Live: https://evoluteur.github.io/repo-atlas/ · permalink per user: ?u=<username> The map. Every public repo as a disc (area ∝ stars), grouped into regions of repos that share topics. Hover for details, click to open the repo. Groups by stars. The legend ranks the regions by the stars they hold, so you see where the attention actually sits. Highlights. The most-starred repo in each group as a card, with its description, language and live-demo link. Hover a card to find its group on the map; the share card lists the top three. Stars over time. Without a token: stars held today, stacked by the year each repo was born. With a token: real cumulative star history per group, from stargazer dates. Share. A 1200×630 card for social posts and a permalink. Each repo's topics are normalised (plurals folded, generic tags like javascript , svg , ui dropped) and hyphenated topics also contribute their parts ( sacred-geometry → sacred , geometry ). Tokens are weighted by inverse document frequency across the account. Tokens used once, or by more than 45% of repos, carry no signal and are dropped. Repos with almost no topics fall back to description words. Repos are compared by cosine similarity and merged bottom-up (average linkage) until no two groups are more than 0.16 alike. The eight groups holding the most stars get a color and a two-word name (the tokens most frequent inside the group and rarest outside it). Everything else folds into loners . All of this is in src/atlas.js : pure functions, no DOM, tested with node --test . Everything runs in the browser against the public GitHub REST API. The map and the highlights work anonymously (60 requests/hour per IP; a typical account takes 2). GitHub only lists when each star was given to authenticated callers, so the star-history chart needs a token. A fine-grained token with no extra permissions is enough. It is kept in sessionStorage for the tab and only sent to api.github.com . Big repos are sampled: every stargazer page for repos under 500 stars, otherwise the first, last and three evenly spaced pages. Each fetched star is an exact (count, date) point; months in between are interpolated. Results are cached in localStorage (repos 1 hour, star history 24 hours). If the API can't be reached (rate limit, offline), the page lets you paste the JSON from api.github.com/users/<login>/repos?per_page=100 and maps that instead. No build step. Serve the folder and open it: npx serve . # or: python3 -m http.server open http://localhost:3000/ ? u=evoluteur npm test # clustering, highlights and timeline math npm run build # dist/repo-atlas.html: one self-contained file index.html page shell src/atlas.js clustering, highlights, timelines (pure, Node-testable) src/github.js REST client: repos, sampled stargazer pages src/charts.js D3: circle-pack map, birth-year columns, stacked sta
